hints: Focus on what has to be broken when a liquid boils, intermolecular forces between molecules, not bonds inside molecules.
Remember nitrogen is small and very electronegative, so $\text{NH}_3$ can form strong $\text{N-H} \cdots \text{N}$ attractions, while phosphorus is larger and much less electronegative.
Compare the strength of that special intermolecular force in ammonia with the much weaker permanent dipole forces in phosphine to see which needs more energy to separate.
walkthrough:
**What boiling really breaks**

Boiling separates whole molecules from each other. It overcomes intermolecular forces, it does not break covalent bonds inside the molecule.

So we compare: intermolecular forces in $\text{NH}_3$ vs in $\text{PH}_3$

**Check hydrogen bonding ability**

Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to N, O or F, plus a lone pair on N, O or F of a neighbour.

$$\text{N-H} \cdots \text{:N}$$ 
In $\text{NH}_3$, N is small, very electronegative and has a lone pair, so this condition is met perfectly.

**Compare with phosphine**

In $\text{PH}_3$, P is in Period 3, larger and much less electronegative than N. The $\text{P-H}$ bond is almost non-polar, so there is no significant hydrogen bonding.

$\text{PH}_3$ has only weaker permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces and London forces.

**Link to boiling point**

Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than ordinary dipole forces. More energy is needed to separate $\text{NH}_3$ molecules.

Therefore $\text{NH}_3$ has the higher boiling point because of significant hydrogen bonding.

options.A: Both molecules are polar and pyramidal in shape. $\text{PH}_3$ does have a dipole, just a much weaker one, so polarity alone does not explain the large difference.
options.B: Correct. $\text{NH}_3$ forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds ($\text{N-H} \cdots \text{N}$) because N is small, highly electronegative and has a lone pair. $\text{PH}_3$ cannot, so only has weaker dipole and London forces, giving it a lower boiling point.
options.C: Boiling does not break $\text{N-H}$ or $\text{P-H}$ covalent bonds, only the forces between molecules. Stronger covalent bonds inside the molecule do not raise the boiling point.
options.D: This is factually wrong. Both $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{PH}_3$ have a pyramidal shape with one lone pair on the central atom. The difference is that only the N lone pair can take part in effective hydrogen bonding.
